one_liner: GPL-3 C base64 codec with SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512 VBMI/Neon kernels; author's tables beat Chrome's codec 7-11x, aklomp 11-70%.
what_it_does: A small C library (about ten .c files, extern "C" header turbob64.h) that encodes and decodes standard RFC 4648 base64: size_t tb64enc(in, inlen, out) and tb64dec(in, inlen, out) write into a caller-allocated buffer and return the output length, with 0 meaning invalid input (or empty input); tb64enclen/tb64declen size the buffers. On first call it detects the CPU and routes to scalar, SSSE3, AVX, AVX2 or AVX-512 VBMI kernels; each kernel is also exported (tb64v256enc, tb64xdec, ...), and _tb64e/_tb64d function pointers skip the dispatch check. Only the '+/' alphabet with '=' padding is handled: there is no base64url (issue #25 open), no MIME line-break or whitespace skipping and no streaming/incremental API.
how_it_is_fast: The SIMD kernels follow Mula and Lemire's AVX2 base64 method (arXiv 1704.00605, cited in the source): pshufb splits 3-byte groups, mulhi/mullo shifts unpack 6-bit fields, and a pshufb offset table maps them to ASCII. Decode uses aqrit's hashed-LUT variant (avg_epu8 + two pshufb lookups), with maddubs/madd to pack 6-bit values back into bytes. The AVX-512 VBMI path does encode with vpermb + vpmultishiftqb, per Mula's AVX-512 notes. Loops are unrolled 128-256 bytes with software prefetch. By default only part of the input is validated (in the AVX2 main loop, 1 of every 4 32-byte vectors), which removes most of the check work. The fast scalar path (tb64x) uses an 8 KB 12-bit encode table and four 1 KB decode tables.
when_to_use: x86-64 servers with AVX-512 VBMI (Ice Lake or later, Zen 4/5) moving 10 KB to multi-MB standard-base64 blobs, where GPL-3 or a commercial license is acceptable. The author's Ryzen 9 7950X table shows 77.6/76.7 GB/s at 1 MB, against 45.3/46.7 GB/s for its own AVX2 path. On Zen 5 in base64-turbo's harness it still leads at 10 MB (37.7/55.8 vs 29.4/45.7 GiB/s).
AVX2-only machines where you want more than aklomp/base64 or fastbase64 give. On the author's i7-9700K, tb64v256 beats aklomp b64avx2 by 11%/32% (encode/decode) at 1 MB and 18%/70% at 50 KB.
Apple M1 or other aarch64 targets built with clang: the M1 50 KB table shows 24.0/15.4 GB/s against aklomp's neon64 at 19.1/12.5.
CPUs with no usable SIMD path (the RISC-V build is scalar only): the tb64x scalar codec runs 6.5/5.5 GB/s at 1 MB on the i7-9700K, against Chrome's scalar codec at 2.5/4.3.
when_not_to_use: You can't ship GPL-3 and won't buy a license. ClickHouse dropped it for aklomp/base64 in Sept 2023 (PR 54119) over GPL-3 and its non-thread-safe initialization, and accepted slower base64 in exchange.
You need base64url (JWT, URLs), MIME/PEM line breaks, whitespace tolerance or forgiving decoding. None is supported, and tb64dec rejects any input over 20 bytes whose length is not a multiple of 4.

You rely on the decoder to reject every malformed input. The default build checks only part of the input, so corrupted characters in the unchecked parts decode to garbage without an error. Full checking needs make FULLCHECK=1, and the CMake FULLCHECK option is broken (it defines DB64CHECK instead of B64CHECK).

Memory-safety-sensitive code run under ASAN/fuzzers with exact-size buffers. Open issue #26 (Sept 2024, no reply) reports tb64enc reading past in+inlen and writing past tb64enclen(inlen) for inlen=94.
You need independently reproducible cross-library numbers. The competitor harness (xtb64.mak, xb64test.h) is not in the repo, and the README tables were last updated in Aug 2023.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (make builds libtb64.a/libtb64.so; the CMake target is turbo::base64); a handful of .c files, so a source-drop also works
integration.min_toolchain: C (no standard stated). The README lists GCC>=4.6 or Clang>=3.2 on x86, GCC>=6.3 or Clang>=6.0 on aarch64, Xcode>=9, VS2017 and ppc64le GCC>=8. The AVX-512 file needs -mavx512vbmi support; otherwise build with NAVX512=1. The CMake build needs 3.15+.
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with runtime dispatch (scalar, SSSE3, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 VBMI); aarch64 Neon and ppc64le Power9 Altivec chosen at compile time; s390x and big-endian are supported; RISC-V gets only the scalar plus generic v128 build
integration.thread_safety: Encode/decode calls are stateless. The first-call CPU dispatch (tb64ini) sets a plain static flag and global function pointers with no synchronization, so call tb64ini(0,0) once before starting threads. ClickHouse cited this as 'non-threadsafe initialization'.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — standard alphabet and padding only, caller-allocated buffers through a C API, no base64url, no whitespace or line-break handling, no streaming; padding and validation rules differ from strict decoders

gotchas: Buffers: tb64enc does not write a trailing NUL, so allocate tb64enclen(n)+1 if you terminate the output yourself (issue #23). Open issue #26 shows it can also touch bytes past both buffer ends, so leave slack.

Validation is partial unless you build with FULLCHECK=1 through make. A return of 0 means both 'invalid' and 'empty input'. Unpadded inputs of 20 bytes or fewer are decoded best-effort (ClickHouse PR 54119 notes this), while longer ones are rejected.

tb64ini(0,1) turns on the short-string AVX2 mode (_tb64v256*). Its decoder skips most checks and may read up to 32 bytes past the input end, and a ClickHouse bug (PR 31797) had this path leaking the next string's bytes into encoded output. The mode is ignored on AVX-512 machines.

On x86-64 the CMake build compiles the scalar core with -march=native, so the library it produces may not run on older CPUs; the makefile does not do this. README MB/s figures are counted on base64-text size for both encode and decode (issue #11), so raw-byte throughput is 0.75x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over aklomp/base64 (BSD-2; ClickHouse's 2023 replacement) or the research codecs fastbase64/base64simd only when you need the last 10-70% of AVX2 throughput, or its AVX-512 VBMI path, on standard-alphabet data and GPL-3 or a commercial license is fine. In Rust, base64-turbo (0BSD, fully validated, base64url) ties it in cache and trails only on DRAM-sized buffers; simdutf is the choice for base64url or forgiving decoding.
verified_claims_summary: These are the author's own tables, and the competitor harness is not published. On an i7-9700K with gcc 11.2 (2022), the AVX2 path encodes/decodes a 1 MB buffer at 29.1/29.7 GB/s, against 2.5/4.3 for Google Chrome's codec (about 11.4x/6.9x) and 26.2/22.5 for aklomp AVX2; the Ryzen 9 7950X AVX-512 VBMI figures (77.6/76.7 GB/s) have no external row. As a partial outside check, base64-turbo's criterion harness (upstream per-file flags, default partial-check build) measured it at 80.7/107.8 GiB/s at 64 KiB on Zen 5 EPYC 9R45, against 13.5/27.9 for Rust's base64 crate.
status_note: The codec itself has not changed since the Aug 2023 release. Later commits (2025-2026) are contributor build fixes for Apple Silicon and RISC-V, and the 2024 ASAN report is still unanswered. It is GPL-3 with a commercial license on request, and small enough to vendor if the license works for you.
